english: Just one more penalty left. If Gonzalo Montiel scores, Argentina are world champions.

In midfield, the captain waits, arm in arm with his teammates. He is thirty-five. He has lost four finals with Argentina and, six years earlier, said goodbye to the national team. This World Cup final in Qatar is maybe the last chance.
Montiel steps up and the captain looks at the sky. The same sky he points to after almost every goal, for his grandmother.
Twenty-five years earlier, a doctor in Rosario saw that he was barely growing. And every night, the boy stuck a needle in his leg.
Almost four years after Qatar, Argentina played another World Cup final. Two days later, he sat down and wrote a short note. In it, two words in Spanish. Me vacié. I emptied myself.
He never talked much. He just played. How did a quiet boy who was too small end up carrying a country? It all began on a little pitch in Rosario, one afternoon when a kids' team was one player short.
In that note, he also thanked his family. Without them there would have been no career. And the first to believe in him was his grandmother.
It was a small neighbourhood club, Grandoli, in Rosario, Argentina. The coach, Salvador Aparicio, was looking for anyone who could play.
By the touchline stood a lady, Celia, who had come to watch her grandson Matías. She had also brought his little brother, four or five years old.
She pointed at the little one. The coach looked and hesitated. He was tiny, much shorter than the others. But Celia did not give up and insisted he put him in.
At last Aparicio agreed. He put the boy on the wing, next to Celia, and told her: if he cries, take him off.
At first he barely touched the ball. But when the ball came back, he took it with his left foot and went past one kid after another. He didn't cry. Years later, he remembered scoring two goals.
In that game the others were two or three years older. Some were almost twice his size. It didn't seem to matter.
Aparicio never took him off again. And from that day, it was Celia who took him to every training session and match.

That boy was Lionel Andrés Messi. He was born in Rosario on the twenty-fourth of June 1987, the third child of Jorge and Celia. Yes, his mother was also called Celia, like his grandmother. His father worked in a steel factory. His mother, in a small magnet workshop.
He had two older brothers, Rodrigo and Matías. Later, his sister María Sol completed the family.
Rosario is a working-class city on the Paraná river, with factories, a port and two clubs that divide it: Newell's Old Boys and Rosario Central.

The family lived in a simple house in the south of the city, in the La Bajada neighbourhood. The brothers played in the street until dark. Lionel was always the smallest, and always the one with the ball.
He went to a state school near home, School Number 66. Many years later, a mural with his face appeared in the neighbourhood. It says he is from another galaxy, and from this neighbourhood.
At home everyone called him Leo. Later, because he was so small and so fast, his family and teammates gave him another name. La Pulga. The Flea.
His mother said that at home he was a cheeky, stubborn boy. He hated losing, even at cards. But on the pitch that stubbornness made him never give up on a ball.
His father and brothers supported Newell's Old Boys, the red-and-black half of the city. On match days the whole family went to the stadium. Leo already knew where he wanted to play.
At six he joined Newell's Old Boys, the family club. In one of his first games it was six-nil and he scored four.
The kids born in 1987 formed a team Rosario still talks about. They called it "La Máquina del '87", the Machine of 87. For years they almost never lost.
Sometimes opponents asked for a deal before the game: at six-nil, they'd stop. Even winning six-nil, Lionel got angry if he hadn't scored.

A coach, Carlos Marconi, often tells this story. He promised Leo an alfajor, a chocolate biscuit, for every goal. He scored so many that Marconi changed the deal: two alfajores, but only for headers. Soon after, the smallest on the pitch scored a header. He smiled at Marconi and held up two fingers.
His teammates remember details. Before games he cleaned his boots carefully and taped his ankles, like a professional. He was eight or nine.
A teammate recalls a derby against Rosario Central. Leo dribbled past the same defender again and again, until the defender's father shouted from the stand to kick him.
The league recorded his goals: more than two hundred in five years. In Rosario they say the real number was much bigger.
His size was a problem. Bigger defenders kicked him, and some parents shouted for them to stop him. He always got up and asked for the ball again.
Coaches asked him to pass earlier so he wouldn't get hurt. He kept dribbling. If he lost the ball, he went straight to win it back.
But in 1998, when he was ten, his grandmother Celia died. The person who had brought him to football was gone.
Years later he said she was a very great love and that it is still hard for him to talk about her. He dedicates his goals to her. After many of them, he looks up and points to the sky.
His mother said that after Celia's death the boy talked to his grandmother and asked her for help. Few knew. He wasn't one to talk about his feelings.
Without her, he kept playing. He was still the best in the team. But something else was wrong, and everyone could see it. The other kids were growing. He wasn't.
Newell's took him to a hormone doctor, Diego Schwarzstein. They wanted to know why their biggest prospect was so small.
Tests showed little growth hormone in Lionel's body. Without treatment he would end up ten to fifteen centimetres shorter.
One word would follow him for years. Small. The best player of his age in Rosario, and the smallest.
There was a treatment: a small injection every night in the legs. It was very expensive, more than nine hundred dollars a month.
Still a little boy, he learned to inject himself. Every night the same routine: a needle in the leg. A teammate saw him do it before games, as if it were nothing.
A friend's father taught him to drive on a country road. Lionel was only eleven.
Every month his father did the sums. The medicine took a large part of his factory wage. Help from insurance and the club didn't last. Without treatment, his son's football would end before it began.
So they looked for a club that would pay. Lionel had a trial in Buenos Aires, at River Plate, one of the biggest clubs in the country.
In 2026, Messi himself told the story. He trained there about ten days, and River wanted to keep him. They even offered to pay for the treatment. But Newell's had to release him.
He was never so close to playing for a big club in his own country.
But when he asked Newell's to leave, they said no, and River's offer fell through. It all ended there, he said. Then help came from across the ocean.

An Argentine agent in Barcelona was receiving videos of a boy from Rosario. With another agent, he showed them to the club, which invited him for a trial. In September 2000, Lionel and his father flew to Spain. He was thirteen.
At Newell's, his teammates didn't know where he was. They were told he was ill.
In Barcelona he played against older boys. The sporting director, Carles Rexach, came to watch.
It is said Rexach would take three or four minutes from his seat to the pitch. He took fifteen, because he couldn't take his eyes off the boy.
At that trial was Cesc Fàbregas, who would be Messi's teammate for years. A coach told him to mark the new Argentine, and hard.
Cesc looked at him and thought it would be easy. He was tiny. Seconds later, he was on the ground, and the Argentine was off with the ball.
Rexach said he told the club: sign him, without thinking twice. But those in charge had doubts. He was foreign, very small and needed expensive treatment. Weeks passed and no one decided.
For Jorge, the wait was terrible. He had left a secure job at the factory. He was living in a hotel with his son, in a foreign city, not knowing if they would have a home there.
After more than two months, Jorge called Rexach and was clear: if it wasn't settled now, they were going home.
On the fourteenth of December 2000, Rexach met the agents at a tennis club. With no paper to hand, he wrote a promise on a napkin: Barcelona would sign Lionel Messi.
A club official, Joan Gaspart, admitted the napkin had no legal value. It was to calm a father about to leave. And it worked.
Rexach signed, and the agents were witnesses. The napkin was later auctioned in London for more than seven hundred and sixty thousand pounds.
Barcelona would pay for the treatment and give the father a job. In February 2001, they all moved to Spain.
At thirteen, Leo didn't fully understand it all. He knew he would play and that the injections would go on, now paid by Barcelona.
For the boy from La Bajada it was a dream. For the family, the start of the hardest year of their lives.
Nothing went as they imagined. Because of the rules for foreigners, Lionel spent months without official games. And in only his second game in the youth team, he broke his leg.
His mother, brothers and sister missed home. They didn't adapt and, still in the first year, decided to go back to Rosario.
Jorge asked his son if he wanted to go back. Lionel said no. Years later he put it in one sentence: I wanted to keep going, and my dad stayed with me.
The family was split across two continents. Lionel and his father stayed in Barcelona, living on part of Jorge's salary. The rest went to his wife and children in Rosario.
Now a thirteen-year-old boy lived eleven thousand kilometres from his mother, brothers and little sister.
On Sundays there was no one. He played video games with his father in the flat. Then, says biographer Guillem Balagué, he went to his room to cry into his pillow.
My old man was always with me, Messi said, and we went through a lot of ugly things together.
At the club he hardly spoke. At the first training, when asked his position, he murmured one word, "forward", and sat in a corner of the dressing room.
His teammates didn't know what to think. Fàbregas said that for a long time they thought he couldn't speak. He could. He was just very shy. He didn't say much. He just played.
They called him "el enano", the dwarf. But when the ball reached him, nobody laughed.

Little by little he found his place. The team was full of 1987 kids like him: Cesc Fàbregas, Gerard Piqué and others. They played with three at the back and always attacked, and came to be called the Baby Dream Team.
Little by little the quiet boy began joking with teammates. In fact he was funny and loved cards and video games. He hated losing at them as much as at football.
One season they hardly lost, and Messi scored more than thirty goals. Piqué, much taller, protected him on the pitch.

The coach, Tito Vilanova, would be one of the most important people in Messi's life. The story goes that in one game they were three-nil up after three minutes. Tito joked with his assistant: what do we tell them at half-time, at eight-nil?
The injections continued every night. And each year he grew a little. By his teens, the treatment had worked.
He would end up about one metre seventy. Still one of the shortest on the pitch. But tall enough.
Many years later, his Rosario doctor, Diego Schwarzstein, was clear: he only helped a boy grow. Everything else was Messi's own work.
In November 2003, Barcelona played in Porto at the opening of a stadium. The coach, Frank Rijkaard, brought on a sixteen-year-old youth player, Lionel Messi. On the other bench was José Mourinho.
It was only a friendly. But the boy had now played for the first team. That season he rose through four of the club's teams, one by one.
His official debut was on the sixteenth of October 2004, against Espanyol. He came on at the end, wearing number thirty. He was seventeen.
He was then Barcelona's youngest ever player in the Spanish league. Others broke the record later. He would stay at the club seventeen years.
At the club they remember him as so shy he hardly spoke. One agent had never seen such thin legs on a footballer.
But in the dressing room someone already knew what he could do. Ronaldinho, the best in the world, protected the quiet boy.

The Brazilians Deco, Sylvinho and Thiago Motta also looked after the shy kid. Ronaldinho sat next to him in the dressing room and took him to the Brazilians' table. Leo says he learned from all of them, above all from him.
Not everyone was like that. The Frenchman Ludovic Giuly recalls that some veterans kicked the kid in training to see how he reacted. He didn't complain. He got up and carried on.
On the first of May 2005, against Albacete, Messi came on at the end. Ronaldinho lifted the ball over the defence and Messi chipped it over the goalkeeper. Offside, said the referee.
Moments later, Ronaldinho did exactly the same. And Messi did exactly the same again. This time the goal counted.
Ronaldinho bent down and the boy jumped onto his back. First official goal for Barcelona. Ronaldinho is proud to have been at the start of this story.

I'll stop here for a moment. Something about me: I'm Kamil. I'm twenty-one and I've been making YouTube channels since 2014, when I was nine. Almost all of them failed. A hundred thousand subscribers and the silver button are my childhood dream. If this story means something to you, subscribe: I get one step closer. Back to the story.
In spring 2006, in the Champions League knockouts, Messi ran rings round Chelsea at Stamford Bridge. Two weeks later, in the second leg, he injured his thigh and left in tears.
The whole Camp Nou stood to applaud him. Rijkaard hugged him. Messi was eighteen.
Barcelona won the final in Paris. Messi didn't play. He was so sad he didn't join the celebrations. Years later he said he deeply regretted that night.
In 2004 another question had come up. Messi had lived in Spain since he was thirteen, and the Spanish federation wanted him to play for Spain.
The Argentine coaches found out and acted fast. In June 2004 they arranged an under-20 friendly with Paraguay, mainly so Messi would play and be tied to the country.
Argentina won eight-nil. Messi admits playing for Spain was quite possible. But in his heart he was from Rosario.

Cesc Fàbregas, an old friend from the academy, says it would have been phenomenal to see Leo play for Spain. Years later Spain won the World Cup without him. Argentina's national team would wait eleven more years for a title.

In 2005, at the under-20 World Cup in the Netherlands, he was the best player of the tournament. He scored six goals, including two penalties in the final against Nigeria. Argentina were world champions.
He won the tournament's Golden Ball and Golden Boot, for best player and top scorer. For the first time, the boy from Rosario was a champion in blue and white.
Six weeks later, in August 2005, he made his senior debut, in a friendly in Budapest against Hungary. He came on in the second half.

At his first touch, a defender grabbed his shirt. Messi pulled his arm free, and his arm hit the defender. The referee showed him red. He had been on the pitch less than a minute. It is said he left in tears.
Years later he said what he thought: I came on, they sent me off, and they'll never call me up again.
That night a teammate ran to protest to the referee for him. His name was Lionel Scaloni. Remember this name: years later he will come back into this story.
They called him up again. In March 2006, against Croatia, he scored his first goal for Argentina. And that summer he went to his first World Cup, in Germany.
Against Serbia and Montenegro he came on and scored the sixth goal in a six-nil. At eighteen he was the youngest Argentine to score at a World Cup.
He also set up a goal for Hernán Crespo. It already looked like this was his place.
In the quarter-finals, against hosts Germany, Argentina were winning. But the coach made his last changes with other players, and the game slipped away. They lost on penalties.
Messi stayed on the bench the whole game. For the first time, a World Cup ended with him only watching. He said nothing to the press. Once again he spoke little.
In April 2007, in the Copa del Rey semi-final against Getafe, Messi picked up the ball in his own half. He went past one, then another, then another, then the goalkeeper, and scored.
He started on the right, near the halfway line. In about ten seconds he crossed almost the whole pitch, ball glued to his left foot.
All of Argentina recognised that goal. It was almost the same as Diego Maradona's, Argentina's greatest hero, against England at the 1986 World Cup. Messi was nineteen.
Barcelona won five-two. But in the second leg Getafe won four-nil and Barcelona went out. Not even a goal like that saved the team.
These were hard years at Barcelona. Ronaldinho was fading, the team was losing and the club wanted a fresh start. Messi improved every month, but got injured a lot.

In the note he wrote after the 2026 final, there is another sentence: I swear I always gave everything. And it was true. But for many years with the national team, giving everything was not enough to win.
In summer 2007, at the Copa América in Venezuela, Argentina reached the final against Brazil. Messi had just turned twenty. Brazil won three-nil.
He played the ninety minutes and could do almost nothing. At the end he had to watch Brazil celebrate.
It was his first final for the senior team. No one imagined he would lose three more before winning one.
In 2008 he wanted to play at the Beijing Olympics. Barcelona refused to release him: the Games weren't on football's official calendar. The case went to a sports court.
Messi said the choice was his and there would be no other Games. The court sided with the clubs.
But Barcelona had a new coach, Pep Guardiola. He had been Olympic champion in Barcelona in 1992, and he understood. He let him go.
At the Games he scored two: against Ivory Coast and the Netherlands.

In the final against Nigeria, in front of about ninety thousand people, he put his friend Ángel Di María through, who chipped the ball over the goalkeeper. It was the only goal. Argentina won Olympic gold.

He said afterwards that some things in football happen only once in a lifetime. And it was his only Games. He says that gold is one of the wins he values most. And in Barcelona, Guardiola was going to give him a new role.
Guardiola began with a surprise: he told Ronaldinho, Messi's idol, that he wasn't counting on him. The team would revolve around a twenty-one-year-old.
That summer Ronaldinho went to Milan and told Leo to keep the number ten shirt. The quiet boy who had jumped on his back now had his number and was the star.
In May 2009, Barça went to the Bernabéu to face Real Madrid. A book by Martí Perarnau says that the day before, Guardiola called Messi to his office and showed him a video.
Between Real's midfielders and defenders there was a gap. Guardiola asked him to start on the right and move into it, through the middle. With the ball, run at goal.
According to the book, Guardiola kept it secret until the last moment.
Messi was neither a winger nor a striker. He stayed somewhere in the middle, and the defenders didn't know who should follow him. Barcelona won six-two in Madrid. Messi scored two.
Days later, in the semi-final at Stamford Bridge, Barcelona were losing in the ninety-third minute. Messi passed to Andrés Iniesta, who scored. Barcelona were in the final.
Three weeks later, in Rome, the Champions League final was against Manchester United. Beforehand, Guardiola showed a video of the season with music from Gladiator.
Before that final, Leo remembered Paris, the night he felt left out and missed the party. This time, he said, he had to enjoy it more.
In the seventieth minute, Xavi crossed into the box. And the smallest on the pitch jumped above the defenders and headed over the tall Van der Sar.
Van der Sar was almost two metres. Messi, about one metre seventy. The boy who was too small beat him in the air.
Barcelona won two-nil.
That year they won everything there was to win. League, Cup, Champions League and three more trophies. Six out of six, which no team had done.
The sixth came in December, in Abu Dhabi, against Argentina's Estudiantes. In extra time Messi decided it with his chest.
Weeks earlier he had won his first Ballon d'Or, the award for best in the world. He was twenty-two. The boy who was too small was now the best.
In January 2011, at the Ballon d'Or gala in Zurich, the three finalists all came from the same school: La Masia, Barcelona's academy. Xavi, Andrés Iniesta and Lionel Messi.
Almost everyone bet on Xavi or Iniesta, world champions with Spain. Iniesta had even scored the winner in the final. But Messi won, for the second year running.
He said he didn't expect it. And that Xavi and Iniesta deserved it as much as he did, or even more. They were the first to congratulate him.
The three gave a press conference together and said the same thing: the award belonged to the team.
Years later Xavi recalled meeting him on a trip: a polite kid, humble, not vain at all. He never imagined he would become the best player in history.

In May 2011, at Wembley, Barcelona beat Manchester United in another Champions League final. Messi scored with a low shot from outside the box. The most moving moment came at the end. That spring, defender Éric Abidal had had surgery for a liver tumour. Carles Puyol gave him the armband so that Abidal would lift the trophy.

In May 2012, Guardiola said goodbye to Camp Nou as coach. Messi scored all four goals and, after the fourth, ran to the touchline to hug him. Guardiola joked: Leo stole the spotlight all season, and you couldn't even be jealous.
In December 2012 he broke a forty-year-old record. Gerd Müller had scored eighty-five goals in a calendar year. Messi reached ninety-one, five of them in a single Champions League game.

Müller wasn't upset. He called him a giant and joked: his only flaw was not playing for Bayern. Weeks later, Leo sent him a Barça shirt on which he wrote by hand: my respect and admiration, a hug. For Leo, titles were worth more than records.
Life off the pitch had changed too. His girlfriend was Antonela Roccuzzo, from Rosario, whom he had known since childhood. In November 2012 their first son, Thiago, was born.
Two months after Thiago's birth, Leo said being a father changes a person completely. Now his son came first.

In January 2013 he won his fourth Ballon d'Or in a row, something never seen before. But that winter Tito Vilanova was again being treated for cancer. He had been his coach at La Masia and now ran the first team. And Abidal had barely returned from a liver transplant. In Zurich, Leo forgot to thank them, and later apologised. Tito, he once said, believed in him when he was a kid nearly always on the bench.
At Barcelona he was a god. With the national team, the story was very different.
Argentina hadn't won a major title since 1993, when Messi was six. Now a whole country was counting on him.

At the 2010 World Cup in South Africa, the coach was Maradona himself. In the quarter-finals, in Cape Town, Germany scored after three minutes and won four-nil. Messi didn't score in the whole tournament.
After the game, Maradona said he saw Messi crying in the dressing room.
And whoever says he doesn't feel this shirt, he said, is stupid.
Because that is exactly what many in Argentina were saying. He had gone to Spain at thirteen. He didn't play for an Argentine club. He didn't even sing the anthem before games.
They had a name for it: "pecho frío". Cold chest. Someone who doesn't feel enough when it counts. For many, his silence showed lack of interest.
At the 2011 Copa América, at home, the fans booed him. His father said his son was hurt and didn't understand why they whistled at him.

At that Copa, coach Sergio Batista wanted to use him as at Barcelona. It didn't work. Messi said it was a mistake to compare the national team with Barcelona, a team that had played together for years.
Argentina went out in the quarter-finals, on penalties, against Uruguay. At home the criticism didn't stop. So he did what he always did. He spoke little. He just played.
In April 2014, Tito Vilanova died, aged forty-five. Six days earlier, his former assistant says, Leo visited him at home and they talked for hours. The coach of his first great team was gone.

Less than two months later, at the World Cup in Brazil, Messi carried the team. At the first goal, against Bosnia, he looked at the sky, as so often. He scored four goals in the group stage, including the winner against Iran in the ninety-first minute.
He was named man of the match four times. And Argentina were back in the final, twenty-four years later.
In the semi-final they beat the Netherlands on penalties. Defender Javier Mascherano said that without Leo they would never have got so far.
The final was at the Maracanã, in Rio, again against Germany. Messi and his teammates had chances. No one scored. Until, in extra time, Mario Götze scored.
At the end Messi received the World Cup Golden Ball, for the tournament's best player. On the way to the award he walked right past the trophy without looking at it.
He said that award didn't interest him. The then FIFA president, Sepp Blatter, later said Messi kept repeating to himself: the best, but not the champion.
Second lost final. Three years later he said he would never forget this defeat.

In 2015, at the Copa América in Chile, Argentina were back in the final. Against Chile it was nil-nil after a hundred and twenty minutes. Messi scored his penalty. Two teammates missed, and Chile won.
A month earlier, with Barcelona, he had won the Champions League again, in Berlin, alongside Neymar and Luis Suárez. At club level he won everything. With the national team, he always lost.
Chile's coach was Argentine: Jorge Sampaoli. Two years later he would be Argentina's coach.
Messi then wrote that there is nothing more painful in football than losing a final. And he was already on three.
In June 2016, a new chance: a special Copa América in the United States, a hundred years after the first. The final was at MetLife Stadium, near New York.
And the opponent was Chile again. Again no one scored. Again it all went to penalties.
Messi took the first penalty. He leaned back and shot high, over the bar.
Chile won on penalties. Fourth lost final with Argentina. Three in a row, in three years.
Lucas Biglia also had his penalty saved. But everyone remembers the captain's.
Minutes later, in the tunnel, a journalist stopped him. The quiet man said just a few words: it's over, for me the national team is over.
The team was devastated. Sergio Agüero, his best friend, shared a room with him for years at almost every camp. The defeat, he said, destroyed Leo.
Messi cried on his shoulder for about twenty-five seconds, like a little boy, repeating: this isn't for me, it isn't for me.
Later, the fitness coach says, he found Leo awake at two in the morning, sobbing.

Then something unexpected happened. In Argentina people asked him to stay. The president called him and said publicly that Messi was the best the country had. On a rainy Saturday in Buenos Aires, hundreds gathered at the Obelisk with signs. "Don't go, Leo."
Somewhere in Argentina, fifteen-year-old Enzo Fernández also wrote to him asking him to stay. Six years later he would play beside him in a World Cup final.
The country that had called him cold now wanted him back. Less than two months later he announced his return. In the first game, he scored.
They asked him why. He said he loved the country and this shirt too much, and wanted to help.
Later he explained why he wanted to quit: not only because of the defeat, but because of things outside football that hurt him and his family.
He even said he didn't know whether he had told his father before saying it in the tunnel. He just felt that, at that moment, it had to be that way.
That summer a Spanish court convicted Messi and his father of tax fraud over image rights. The prison sentence became a fine, as is usual there for a first time.
In court, Messi said the money was his father's business. The family had already paid back about five million euros.

In June 2017, Leo married Antonela in Rosario, where they both grew up. He could have married anywhere but chose his home town. About two hundred and fifty guests came, with teammates from Barça and the national team. Thiago and his little brother Mateo sat in the front row, and Leo's brothers were witnesses.

Argentina were in trouble. Going into the last game, they weren't even in a qualifying place for the 2018 World Cup. They had to win in Quito, high in the Andes, where they hadn't won for sixteen years.

That night the streets of Argentina were almost empty. People watched in bars and at home. In La Plata, U2 delayed their concert so fans could watch the game on giant screens. In the very first minute Ecuador scored, and the bars went quiet.
And then Messi scored three goals. Argentina won three-one and were going to Russia. Even Ecuador's fans applauded him.
In the dressing room they sang against the critics. Mascherano said missing the World Cup would have ended the story for many.
Messi later said it would have been madness for Argentina not to be at the World Cup. Now, he said, they had peace.
The coach, Jorge Sampaoli, said a line that stuck: Messi doesn't owe Argentina a World Cup. Football owes Messi a World Cup.
Russia didn't pay that debt. In the first game, against Iceland, he missed a penalty.
The goalkeeper, Hannes Halldórsson, also made films in Iceland. He said he had studied Messi's penalties.
They lost three-nil to Croatia. Then they beat Nigeria with a Messi goal; he spoke of enormous relief.
In the round of sixteen, against France, in Kazan, Antonela brought Thiago and Mateo, in shirts saying Daddy. Argentina lost four-three. Messi came home with nothing again.

In the 2026 farewell note, he also wrote that leaving the national team was a decision that hurt, and still hurts, deep in his soul. He had felt that pain once before, at Barcelona. And there, the end began on European nights nobody at the club wants to remember.
Things were starting to break. In 2018 they thrashed Roma in the first leg and then lost three-nil in Rome. A year later, the same: three-nil against Liverpool at home, and four-nil in Liverpool.
Days after Anfield, he said it wasn't the coach's fault. It was mainly his and his teammates'.
In 2019 he won his sixth Ballon d'Or, a record. But that didn't heal what was breaking around him.
In August 2020, in Lisbon, Bayern Munich beat Barça eight-two.
Ten days after Lisbon, Messi sent the club an official letter. He wanted to leave. Barcelona refused: the contract didn't allow it.
His father went to Barcelona to talk with the club. In the end Messi agreed to stay one more year: he would never take the club he loved to court.
About six weeks later, Barcelona let go Luis Suárez, one of his best friends. Leo wrote that Suárez deserved a dignified farewell, not to be thrown out like that. But nothing surprised him any more.
In November 2020 Diego Maradona died. Argentina mourned him for days. Gone was the man who had defended Messi after Cape Town, and the country still had no major title with Messi.
That year the pandemic shut the world indoors. In summer 2021 the Copa América moved to Brazil at the last minute. The final was at the Maracanã, against Brazil.
Because of the pandemic there were almost no fans. One of the biggest games of his life for the national team would be played almost in silence.
The players hadn't seen their families for weeks. Before the final, in the dressing room, the captain who spoke little stood up. Someone filmed it.
For years people thought he was too quiet to be a leader. That night he found his voice.

Forty-five days without seeing our families, lads, he told them. He spoke of goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez, who had become a father and hadn't yet held his daughter. And he finished: let's go out confident and calm, because we're taking this one home.
Martínez said it made him want to cry. Another player said that soon after he was already crying and didn't remember the rest.
In the twenty-second minute, Rodrigo De Paul sent Ángel Di María through, the friend Messi had set up for the Olympic gold goal. Di María chipped the ball over the goalkeeper. One-nil.
For the next seventy minutes Brazil attacked and Argentina held on. Messi missed the chance for a second. It didn't matter.
At the final whistle Messi fell to his knees and covered his face. His teammates ran to him and jumped on top of him until he disappeared.
Then he called his wife and children, in Rosario. After four lost finals he was at last a champion with the senior team, at thirty-four.
At the end Di María said the curse had to end one day, and finally it had. Messi dedicated the title to his family, the Argentine people and Maradona, who was surely supporting them, wherever he was.
A month later he was going to renew with Barcelona. But the club announced that, because of its debts and the Spanish league's rules, it couldn't keep him.
On the eighth of August 2021, he walked into a room at Camp Nou to say goodbye. Before saying anything he started to cry.
He said he wasn't ready. He and his family wanted to stay. He had arrived in that city at thirteen and was leaving at thirty-four, with three sons, Thiago, Mateo and Ciro, all born there.
It also hurt him not to say goodbye to the fans in the stadium. Because of the pandemic he hadn't seen them for a year and a half.
He signed for Paris Saint-Germain. It never worked. When the team lost, he was booed.
Once, after a defeat, he went to Saudi Arabia on a promotional trip without permission. Paris suspended him and he apologised in a video. Everyone already knew he would leave.

In November 2022 Argentina arrived at the World Cup in Qatar thirty-six games unbeaten. The coach was Scaloni, the teammate who had defended him in Budapest. Messi was thirty-five. Everyone knew: it might be the last.
In the first game, against Saudi Arabia, he scored a penalty. Then the Saudis scored two in five minutes. Two-one. It was one of the biggest shocks in World Cup history.
Afterwards Messi went to speak to the journalists. There are no excuses, he said. The dressing room was crushed. But he asked Argentines to trust them: we'll be more united than ever.
His teammates said he had never spoken to them so much. The quiet captain now spoke up loudly.
And a song followed them everywhere: Muchachos. The players sang it on the bus and in the dressing room, with Messi.
From then on, every game was a final. Against Mexico Messi scored first: two-nil. Then Poland and Australia.
Against Australia he played the thousandth game of his career, and scored.
In the quarter-finals, against the Netherlands, Argentina were two-nil up and they equalised in the last seconds. On penalties Argentina won.
There the world saw a Messi never seen before. During an interview a Dutch player walked past, and Messi said to him, Rosario-street style: "What are you looking at, fool?"

The player they had called cold was boiling. In the semi-final, three-nil against Croatia. Messi scored a penalty and then dribbled past one of the best young defenders in the world and set up Julián Álvarez.
On the eighteenth of December 2022, Argentina played the final against France. Messi scored a penalty. Di María got the second.
Two-nil. Ten minutes left. Four lost finals behind him, and the trophy was right there.
Then, in less than two minutes, Mbappé scored two goals. Two-two.
Extra time. Messi scored again. Three-two. And Mbappé scored again, from a penalty. Three-three.
In the last minute France had one more chance, but Martínez stopped it with his leg. After a hundred and twenty minutes, it all went to penalties.
Messi scored. Martínez saved one, and France missed another. Then came Montiel's turn, with the penalty that could win it all.
It was the moment from the start of the film. Montiel went to the ball. Messi looked at the sky. Later he said he was asking God for it to end.
Montiel scored. Lionel Messi fell to his knees on the grass.
He had lost four finals with Argentina. He had said it was the end. He had come back. And now, at thirty-five, he was world champion.
First, the Emir of Qatar put a traditional black robe on his shoulders. Then he lifted the trophy, kissed it and wouldn't let go.
His family came onto the pitch. His mother hugged him. His three sons ran to him. He photographed Antonela with the trophy.

In the final he scored his sixth and seventh goals of the tournament. He again won the World Cup Golden Ball, which eight years earlier hadn't mattered to him, because Argentina had lost. This time he had the trophy.
At that World Cup he was the first to score in the group stage, the round of sixteen, the quarter-final, the semi-final and the final.
Later he said he heard the trophy calling him, as if saying: now you can touch me.
He said he never rewatched the final, only highlights. And that at home his children imitated goalkeeper Martínez's celebrations.
In Buenos Aires millions filled the streets. There were so many that the bus couldn't move, and the players left by helicopter.

In March 2023, before leaving Europe, he had one more happy night in Buenos Aires. In the first home game as world champions, against Panama, at the Monumental, he scored the eight-hundredth goal of his career. He had always dreamed of that, he said: celebrating with his own people, at home.

That summer, with his Paris contract over, he surprised everyone. Not Barcelona, not the huge offer from Saudi Arabia. He chose a young club in the United States, Inter Miami. Many thought he would slow down.
He explained it simply. He wanted to step out of the spotlight a bit and think more about his family. If it were about money, he would have gone to Saudi Arabia.
His first game for Miami was in July 2023. He came on in the second half. In the ninety-fourth minute, at one-one, he curled a free kick into the top corner.
That night he smiled from the bench at Antonela and the children in the stand. LeBron James and Serena Williams were there too. At the goal, David Beckham, the club's co-owner, cried.
Weeks later Miami won the first trophy in its history. Slow down? Not at all. In October, his eighth Ballon d'Or.
In Miami he also became a parent of players. His three sons joined the academy, and he and Antonela cheered them on from the touchline, like the other parents.
In 2024 Argentina reached another Copa América final, against Colombia, in Miami. In the second half his ankle gave way and he had to come off.

On the bench he cried. Teammate Leandro Paredes sat next to him. He said he couldn't even look at him, he could only hear him crying. Argentina won in extra time, without him. It was also the farewell of his friend Di María.

In September 2025 he played what he said was maybe his last home qualifier, in Buenos Aires, against Venezuela. In the warm-up he could barely hold back tears, with more than eighty thousand people shouting his name. He scored two goals. Finishing like this, at home, he said, was his dream.
In December 2025 Miami won the MLS Cup for the first time. On the pitch his son Mateo did keepy-uppies and pointed at his dad.
In March 2026 he scored his nine-hundredth goal. He was thirty-eight, and some thought he was too old.
It came in a game Miami didn't win and which knocked them out of a continental cup. That weighed on him more than the record. And another World Cup was coming.
His father, Jorge, had always wanted to see him play one more World Cup. But shortly before the tournament Jorge became seriously ill. For the first time, Jorge wouldn't be there to watch him.
In the first game, against Algeria, he scored three goals. Then two against Austria and one against Jordan. Argentina won the group comfortably.
And after every game, the same thing. Boots off. Phone in hand. Was there a message from home? That was how he heard about his father.
He didn't say so at the time, but he was playing with his father ill, thousands of kilometres away. Later he admitted he never felt right during the tournament.
In the knockouts every game was a fight. Cape Verde forced extra time.

Against Egypt Messi missed a penalty. He didn't hang his head. He set up a goal for Cristian Romero, scored the equaliser, and Enzo Fernández won it with a header. Against Switzerland, more extra time.
Boots off. Phone. Message from home?

In the semi-final, in Atlanta, it was England. The English scored first. Argentina turned it around in the last five minutes and, in the last one, Messi crossed for the winning goal. Two-one. Another final.
At the end Messi couldn't hold back his emotion. He went round the pitch hugging teammates and staff. Even Scaloni, the coach, was speechless.
He had scored eight goals at that World Cup. No one in history had scored more World Cup goals, or played more games.
The final was on the nineteenth of July 2026, at MetLife Stadium, in New Jersey. The same stadium where, ten years earlier, he had said it was the end.
Before the game, in the dressing room, he asked his teammates to stay calm: forget everything else and think only about playing.
Spain had Lamine Yamal, nineteen, and many young players. They had the ball almost all the time and almost all the chances.
It stayed nil-nil. In a video published later, Messi can be heard telling the team: character, everyone, character.
At the end of ninety minutes, Enzo Fernández, the boy from the letter, was sent off. Ten men, and thirty minutes to hold on.
In the hundred-and-sixth minute, Ferran Torres scored. Argentina couldn't answer.
Messi had only one shot in the game. It was Argentina's fifth lost final.
At the end Messi sat on the grass. Yamal came to hug him. Messi told him to follow his path, that the future belonged to his generation. Yamal said those words were worth a gold medal.
Scaloni cried at the press conference and left the room. Before the final he had said Messi was the best ever to step on a pitch.
The next day Messi wrote to the fans. The pain is immense, he said, and this wound will take time to heal.
Less than three weeks after the final, in August 2026, Jorge Messi died in Rosario after a long illness. He was sixty-eight.
Days later Lionel wrote him a letter and shared it with the world. It began simply. I love you, Dad.

He wrote that he had promised his father to reach the final so he could come and watch it. His father never managed to come. Lionel wanted to win it and bring him the trophy. But he couldn't, he wrote. His legs had nothing left.
He wrote that at the World Cup, after every game, he waited for a message from his father. When it didn't come, he understood how bad things were.
You were father, friend and agent, he wrote. His father left his job in Rosario and waited for a napkin in Barcelona.
Since then, when he looks at the sky, he sees two people there.
On the thirty-first of August he published the note from the start of the film. He had written it on the twenty-first of July, two days after the final, and kept it for six weeks.

In it he said goodbye to the national team. Me vacié, he wrote. I emptied myself. I have nothing more to give, and great young players are coming who deserve their place. Now I'm going to be one more of you.
Later he added: today, after what happened to my father, I'm even more sure of the decision.
He didn't write about trophies or finals. He wrote about his family, the fans and his father.

On the sixth of October 2026 he played his last game for Argentina, a friendly against Benin, at the Monumental in Buenos Aires. River Plate's stadium, the club that once wanted that boy from Rosario and couldn't have him.
About eighty-five thousand people came. He walked out holding hands with his three sons. His mother watched from the stand.
A veteran of the Falklands War sang the anthem. Messi could barely hold back tears. In the tenth minute a long ovation stopped the game, and the Benin players went over to him.
He made two assists and scored a penalty. It was his hundred-and-twenty-sixth goal for Argentina, in his two-hundred-and-eighth game.
The second assist was for Nico Paz, twenty-two, one of those young players he had talked about.
At the end hundreds of drones lit up the sky. And the boy who used to sit silently in a corner of the dressing room took the microphone in front of eighty-five thousand.
First he said he was thinking of his father. Then that it was the saddest day of his career.
For weeks people argued about the refereeing at the World Cup. Messi didn't get into that. That night he said there was nothing strange. The team gave everything.
He said playing for Argentina was the most beautiful thing that could happen. He wanted to stay there his whole life. He told the fans he loved them and would miss them.
He went round the pitch with his wife and sons, and eighty-five thousand sang that Messi wasn't leaving.
He had called it the saddest day of his career. And even so, he had written in the note: I leave in peace, and with pride.
He was too small. Too expensive. A foreigner in Spain and a stranger in Argentina. Later they said he was too old.
Two people believed. His grandmother, who made the coach let him play. And his father, who found the money, crossed the sea and stayed.
He never played just for himself. He played for them. And when he looks at the sky after a goal, it is them he is looking for.
The cold chest Argentina talked about was never cold. He just hid what he felt. He kept it all in and only let it out when he lost, or when he finally won.
And that last final, in July 2026, hurt more than all the others. It wasn't just a trophy. It was the last thing he wanted to bring his father.
Today he still plays in Miami. He has scored more than nine hundred goals. He no longer plays for Argentina. Now, as he wrote, he's just one more fan.
Maybe you are the quiet one. The one in the corner of the dressing room. The one who seems not to care.
Leo was that kid too. He never became loud. He spoke little. He played, for those who believed in him. When it mattered most, he found his voice. One day the whole world was listening to him.
If you're the quiet one, you don't have to shout. Keep playing. Your turn to speak will come.
On the night of his farewell to Argentina, the boy who barely spoke smiled at eighty-five thousand. I'm talking more than ever, he said, and I don't want to leave.
That summer, Spain didn't only end Leo's last World Cup. Two weeks earlier, in Texas, it had ended the dream of another boy, who wanted that trophy so badly.
A boy from a small island in the Atlantic, whom his teammates called crybaby. His name is Cristiano Ronaldo, and his full story is here.
